title: Enterprise topologies
intro: How systems talk to each other: hub-and-spoke, mesh, tree, bus and ring, where each shows up in networks, services, messaging and data, and the products that implement them.
scope: Open source or free to use. The Azure and AWS network services are references because the shapes are most visible there, and are marked as not open source.

groups.label: Topologies
groups.about: The shapes, in plain terms, with where each one shows up.

groups.label: Networks and naming
groups.about: Hubs, transit and the DNS tree.

entries.name: Hub-and-spoke (star)
entries.summary: Every spoke connects to one central hub, and spokes reach each other through it. One place for shared services and control, one place that can fail or become a bottleneck.

started.basis: A general concept, no single start date

version.name: Concept
version.docs: Wikipedia network topology page (first 100,000 of 111,880 characters) and the product docs in Sources

compare.text: Mesh removes the middle: every node can reach others directly. Hub-and-spoke centralises control at the price of a dependency.

notes: Terraform runners and other central CI hubs fit the shape but were not read, so they are not described here (unconfirmed).
The Azure page is dated 2026-04-10 (ms.date). Wikipedia was read for the first 100,000 of 111,880 characters.

sections.title: The shape
items: Every peripheral node connects to a central hub or switch. Adding nodes is simple. The hub is a single point of failure, and in a large cluster the bandwidth into the hub becomes a bottleneck (Wikipedia, network topology).
Spokes do not talk directly. Anything from one spoke to another goes through the hub, which is where inspection, routing and policy sit.

sections.title: Where it shows up
items: Azure hub-spoke: a hub virtual network holds shared services (firewall, VPN or ExpressRoute gateway, Bastion, DNS) and each spoke is a virtual network that isolates a workload. Spokes peer to a single hub in the same region. Peering is nontransitive, so spoke-to-spoke traffic goes through a firewall or router in the hub unless you peer spokes directly.

AWS Transit Gateway: "a network transit hub used to interconnect virtual private clouds (VPCs) and on-premises networks". Attachments (VPCs, VPN, Direct Connect gateway, SD-WAN appliances, peered transit gateways) are associated with route tables.
A central management cluster that controls many workload clusters. Example: one Argo CD registers other clusters with argocd cluster add and deploys to them. See the GitOps topic.

sections.title: Trade-offs
items: Pro: shared services and egress control in one place, workloads isolated from each other, easy to add a spoke. Azure lists central control over security and connectivity as the reason to choose it.

Con: the hub is a shared dependency. Azure advises one hub per region so a failed hub does not break unrelated regions, and warns that firewall bandwidth and the number of peerings limit how many spokes you can add.
Mitigation: second-level hubs, direct spoke peering for high-throughput low-risk traffic (Azure says this can cut firewall cost), or several hubs per region.

entries.name: Mesh
entries.summary: Nodes connect to many other nodes directly. Full mesh links every pair, partial mesh links some. Service meshes, peer-to-peer replication and gossip use the idea.

started.basis: A general concept, no single start date

version.name: Concept
version.docs: Wikipedia network topology page (first 100,000 of 111,880 characters) and the product docs in Sources

compare.text: Hub-and-spoke is cheaper to wire and to govern, but the hub is shared.

notes: The n(n-1)/2 count is arithmetic from the page's statement that connections grow quadratically, not quoted from it.
The Istio page covers sidecar mode only. Ambient mode is only named in its navigation (unconfirmed).

sections.title: The shape
items: Full mesh: every node links to every other node. Connections grow quadratically with the number of nodes, which makes a large full mesh impractical. Partial mesh: some nodes link to two or more others, which gives redundancy without the cost (Wikipedia).
There is no single hub, so no single point of failure by shape, but there is more to configure and more links to secure.

sections.title: Where it shows up
items: Service mesh: every service pod gets a proxy and all traffic between services passes through the sender's and the receiver's proxy. Istio uses Envoy sidecars with a control plane (istiod). Linkerd uses a Rust micro-proxy sidecar. Both give mTLS, retries, load balancing and metrics without changing the application.
Peer-to-peer replication: in Cassandra every replica can accept writes and nodes share membership state by gossip.
Network: Azure Virtual Network Manager can mesh spoke networks directly, and global mesh extends direct connectivity across regions.
AWS Transit Gateway replaces a mesh of VPC peerings with a hub, which is how a full mesh is usually avoided.

sections.title: Trade-offs
items: Pro: no central bottleneck, direct paths, resilience from redundant links.
Con: n(n-1)/2 links for a full mesh. In a service mesh the cost is a proxy per workload and a control plane to run.

entries.name: Hierarchical (tree)
entries.summary: A hierarchy: a root, branches and leaves, where each level delegates to the next. DNS and Prometheus federation are the two examples with docs behind them here.

started.basis: A general concept, no single start date

version.name: Concept
version.docs: Wikipedia network topology page (first 100,000 of 111,880 characters) and the product docs in Sources

notes: RFC 1034 was read for the first 100,000 of 135,972 characters. DNS root servers, caching resolvers' behaviour and later RFCs (such as RFC 1035) were not read.

sections.title: The shape
items: A hierarchy of star networks (Wikipedia). If a link to a leaf fails only that leaf is isolated. If a link to a non-leaf node fails the whole section beneath it is isolated.
Each level only talks to its parent and its children. Authority and data flow up or down the tree.

sections.title: Where it shows up
items: DNS (RFC 1034, November 1987): the name space is a tree of labels. Control of a subtree is delegated at cuts, where NS records name the servers for the subzone. Every zone must be available from at least two servers. Resolvers follow referrals down the tree, and records carry a TTL that limits caching.

Prometheus hierarchical federation: higher-level servers collect aggregated data from many subordinate servers, which helps scale across many data centers. Each Prometheus exposes /federate, which needs at least one match[] selector. Set honor_labels so the source labels are kept.
Organisation wide RBAC and Terraform module trees follow the same shape. They are named in your note and were not read here (unconfirmed).

sections.title: Trade-offs
items: Pro: delegation scales, and an outage stays inside a branch.
Con: the higher up a node is, the more it matters. Cross-branch traffic goes up and back down.

sources.label: RFC 1034: domain names, concepts and facilities

entries.name: Bus
entries.summary: Producers and consumers share one channel. In a messaging system the broker or log is the bus: senders do not know who reads.

started.basis: A general concept, no single start date

version.name: Concept
version.docs: Wikipedia network topology page (first 100,000 of 111,880 characters) and the product docs in Sources

compare.text: A mesh connects services directly through proxies. A bus puts a shared channel between them.

notes: Delivery guarantees (at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once) were not read for any of the three and are not described (unconfirmed).

sections.title: The shape
items: Network bus: all nodes connect to one shared central cable. Cheaper to cable than other shapes, but the cable is a single point of failure (Wikipedia).
A message bus applies the idea in software: producers publish to the bus and consumers subscribe, so they are decoupled in time and in knowledge of each other.

sections.title: Where it shows up
items: Apache Kafka: events are stored in topics split into partitions spread across brokers. Producers write and consumers read, and the two are decoupled. Events with the same key go to the same partition, which keeps their order. Topics keep events for a configurable retention period and consumers can read them repeatedly. Replication copies each partition to several brokers, commonly three.

RabbitMQ (AMQP 0-9-1): publishers send to exchanges, bindings copy messages into queues, consumers subscribe. Exchange types are direct, fanout, topic and headers. A message leaves the broker only after it is acknowledged, and an unacknowledged message is redelivered.
NATS: messaging by subject with publish/subscribe and request/reply, and persistent streaming through JetStream.

sections.title: Trade-offs
items: Pro: producers and consumers change independently, and new consumers need no change to producers.
Con: the bus is critical infrastructure and ordering, delivery guarantees and schema agreement become your problem. Kafka orders only within a partition.

entries.name: Ring
entries.summary: Nodes form a loop, each knowing its neighbours. In a network the ring is historical; in distributed databases a consistent-hash ring spreads data across nodes.

started.basis: A general concept, no single start date

version.name: Concept
version.docs: Wikipedia network topology page (first 100,000 of 111,880 characters) and the product docs in Sources

notes: The Cassandra page is the 5.0 documentation, labelled a prerelease on the page, with no date. Latest GA release per the download page is 5.0.9 (2026-08-07).
The 'only part of the data moves' point is a general property of consistent hashing and was not on the page read (unconfirmed).

sections.title: The shape
items: Network ring: a daisy chain closed into a loop with data travelling in one direction. Aggregate bandwidth is limited by the weakest link between two nodes (Wikipedia).
Token ring is the historical network example. It is named in your note and was not read here (unconfirmed).

sections.title: Where it shows up
items: Cassandra partitions data with consistent hashing on a token ring. Each physical node owns one or more tokens (vnodes), and a key's replicas are found by walking the ring clockwise until enough distinct nodes are found.

Replication: each partition is copied to several nodes by the keyspace's replication strategy and replication factor. NetworkTopologyStrategy is recommended for production and SimpleStrategy for testing.

Membership: nodes share state by gossip, and each node's phi accrual failure detector decides if peers are up or down. Repair uses read repair, hinted handoff and anti-entropy repair with Merkle trees.
Consistency is tunable per operation (ONE, QUORUM, LOCAL_QUORUM, ALL), and W + R > RF gives overlapping read and write sets.

sections.title: Trade-offs
items: Pro: no single master, data spread evenly, nodes added or removed move only part of the data (a general property of consistent hashing, not a quote from the page).
Con: eventual consistency to reason about, and repair work to run.

entries.name: Point-to-point
entries.summary: The simplest shape: a dedicated link between two endpoints.

started.basis: A general concept, no single start date

version.name: Concept
version.docs: Wikipedia network topology page (first 100,000 of 111,880 characters)

notes: Wikipedia is a general source. The page was read for the first 100,000 of 111,880 characters.

sections.title: Definition
items: "The simplest topology with a dedicated link between two endpoints." Its value grows with the number of potential pairs of subscribers, which the page ties to Metcalfe's Law.
Many point-to-point links between many systems become a mesh, or are replaced by a hub or a bus to cut the number of links.

entries.name: Hybrid
entries.summary: Two or more basic topologies combined. Real enterprise estates are almost always hybrids.

started.basis: A general concept, no single start date

version.name: Concept
version.docs: Wikipedia network topology page (first 100,000 of 111,880 characters)

notes: Wikipedia is a general source. The page was read for the first 100,000 of 111,880 characters.

sections.title: Definition
items: Two or more basic topologies combined so that the result does not match any single standard topology.
Typical combination here: hub-and-spoke networks per region, a service mesh inside each cluster, a message bus between systems, and a tree of Prometheus or DNS servers over the top.

entries.name: Azure hub-spoke and Virtual WAN
entries.summary: Azure's reference architecture for a hub virtual network with spoke virtual networks, customer-managed, with a Microsoft-managed variant on Virtual WAN.

started.basis: Not stated on the page read

cncf.text: Commercial service, not a CNCF project.

compare.text: AWS's managed hub is one service. In Azure you build the hub from firewall and gateway services, or use Virtual WAN.

notes: Included as the Azure reference for the hub-and-spoke shape. It is a service, not open source.

sections.title: Pieces
items: The hub holds Azure Firewall (egress and optionally ingress), a VPN or ExpressRoute gateway, Azure Bastion, DNS and Azure Monitor. Spokes hold workloads and peer to the hub with nontransitive peering.
A hub is a regional resource: one hub per region. The page says this recommended Cloud Adoption Framework topology is also the base of Azure landing zones.

Azure Virtual Network Manager groups networks and builds the peerings and routes for you, including direct spoke connectivity and global mesh. Virtual WAN is the Microsoft-managed hub alternative; customer-managed brings cost savings, workload isolation, flexibility and more control over NVAs.

entries.name: AWS Transit Gateway
entries.summary: AWS's regional network hub connecting VPCs, VPNs, Direct Connect and other transit gateways through route tables.

started.basis: Not stated on the page read

cncf.text: Commercial service, not a CNCF project.

version.name: AWS Transit Gateway
version.docs: docs.aws.amazon.com tgw what-is, no version or date on page

notes: The page does not use the words hub-and-spoke or mesh. The link to the shape is the page's own description as a transit hub. Included as a service reference; not open source.

sections.title: Concepts
items: Attachments: VPCs, a Connect SD-WAN or third-party appliance, a Direct Connect gateway, a peering connection with another transit gateway, a VPN connection or concentrator, a Client VPN endpoint, a network function attachment.

Each attachment is associated with exactly one route table, and a route table can have many attachments. Routes propagate from VPCs, VPNs and Direct Connect gateways, and a peering attachment needs a static route.
MTU is 8500 bytes between VPCs, Direct Connect and peering attachments, and 1500 over VPN. Encryption control can enforce encryption in transit for attached VPCs.
Billing: hourly for each attachment, plus traffic processed.

entries.name: DNS
entries.summary: The hierarchical naming system of the internet: a tree of names delegated to name servers, queried by resolvers and cached.

started.basis: RFC 1034 publication (Domain Names - Concepts and Facilities)

cncf.text: Specified by the IETF, not a CNCF project.

notes: RFC 1034 is dated November 1987 and obsoleted RFCs 882, 883 and 973. RFC 1035 was not read.

sections.title: Concepts
items: The name space is a tree. Each node has a label of up to 63 octets, and a domain name is the list of labels from the node to the root, at most 255 octets.

Name servers hold authoritative data organised into zones and may cache data from elsewhere. Delegation happens at cuts, where NS records name the servers for the subzone. Every zone must be available from at least two servers.
Resolvers query name servers for clients and follow referrals. Resource records carry a TTL that limits caching.
Hub-spoke networks usually give all spokes one DNS solution, especially for cross-premises routing and private endpoint records (Azure).

entries.name: Istio
entries.summary: A service mesh: Envoy proxies beside each workload, managed by a control plane called istiod. mTLS, traffic management and telemetry without changing the app. CNCF graduated.

cncf.text: Istio was accepted to CNCF on September 30, 2022 at the Incubating maturity level and then moved to the Graduated maturity level on July 12, 2023.

version.name: Istio
version.docs: istio.io architecture page (the page footer shows 1.31.3)

compare.text: Istio uses Envoy sidecars (and an ambient mode). Linkerd uses its own Rust micro-proxy.

notes: Start date is the first GitHub release. Ambient mode details were not read (unconfirmed).

sections.title: Architecture (sidecar mode)
items: Data plane: Envoy proxies deployed as sidecars, which "mediate and control all network communication between microservices". Envoy is the only component that handles data plane traffic.

Control plane: istiod turns routing rules into Envoy configuration and pushes it at runtime, normalises service discovery for Kubernetes and VMs, and acts as the certificate authority for mTLS between workloads.
Every request passes through the sender's and the receiver's proxy. The mesh gives mTLS and identity based policies, routing, retries, failover and fault injection, and telemetry.

sections.title: Ambient mode
items: The page covers sidecar mode only. Its navigation lists an ambient architecture (ztunnel, waypoints, HBONE), with waypoints described as optional Layer 7 proxies.

entries.name: Linkerd
entries.summary: A service mesh with a purpose built Rust proxy (linkerd2-proxy) as a sidecar and a small control plane. CNCF graduated.

cncf.text: Linkerd was accepted to CNCF on January 23, 2017, moved to the Incubating maturity level on April 6, 2018, and then moved to the Graduated maturity level on July 28, 2021.

version.name: Linkerd
version.docs: linkerd.io architecture page (shows 2.20); version is the latest GitHub release, an edge release

notes: GitHub shows edge releases as the latest. The architecture page names version 2.20. Which releases are open source stable builds was not checked (unconfirmed).
The page does not say mTLS is on by default, only that it is automatic between proxies.

sections.title: Architecture
items: Control plane in the linkerd namespace: the destination service (where to send requests, the TLS identity to expect, policy and service profiles), the identity service (a TLS certificate authority that signs proxy requests, used for proxy-to-proxy mTLS) and the proxy injector (an admission webhook that adds proxy-init and linkerd-proxy to annotated pods).

Data plane: lightweight proxies as sidecars, a native sidecar by default as of 2.20. linkerd2-proxy is a transparent micro-proxy written in Rust. It does HTTP, HTTP/2 and TCP, Prometheus metrics, latency-aware load balancing, and automatic TLS.
In a meshed connection the outbound proxy does discovery, load balancing, circuit breaking, retries and timeouts, and the inbound proxy enforces authorization policy.

entries.name: Apache Kafka
entries.summary: A distributed event streaming platform: producers write events to topics, partitioned and replicated across brokers, and consumers read them independently.

started.basis: GitHub repository created (the project is older: unconfirmed)

cncf.text: An Apache Software Foundation project, not a CNCF project.

version.name: Apache Kafka
version.docs: kafka.apache.org intro and downloads pages (the downloads page lists 4.4.0 released October 22, 2026)

compare.text: Kafka is a durable partitioned log that consumers read at their own position. RabbitMQ routes messages to queues through exchanges and removes them after acknowledgement.

notes: The GitHub repository publishes no GitHub releases, so no automatic release check runs for this entry. The version is from the downloads page.
Consumer groups, KRaft and the log design were not on the introduction page read (unconfirmed).

sections.title: Model
items: An event streaming platform for publishing, subscribing to, storing and processing streams of events. It runs as a cluster of servers: some form the storage layer, the brokers, and the cluster keeps working if a server fails.
Producers write events and consumers read them, decoupled so producers never wait on consumers. Events live in topics with a configurable retention period and can be read repeatedly.
Topics are split into partitions spread across brokers. Events with the same key go to the same partition, which keeps their order. Each partition is replicated, commonly three copies.

entries.name: RabbitMQ
entries.summary: A message broker: publishers send to exchanges, bindings route messages to queues, and consumers acknowledge them.
notes: The licence is not on the page read. The repository's LICENSE was not read. Start date is the oldest GitHub release, which is a 3.5.0 tag, not the project's start. Owned by Broadcom per general knowledge, not on the page (unconfirmed).

sections.title: AMQP 0-9-1 model
items: The broker receives messages from publishers and routes them to consumers. Publishers send to exchanges, which use bindings to copy messages into queues. Consumers subscribe (push, recommended) or poll (pull, usually avoided).

Exchanges: direct (routing key equals binding key), fanout (every bound queue), topic (routing key matched against patterns) and headers (header values, with x-match any or all). The default exchange is an unnamed direct exchange, with every queue bound under its own name.

Acknowledgements: the broker removes a message only after it is acknowledged, and redelivers it if the consumer dies. A consumer can reject a message and ask for a requeue or discard. Prefetch limits unacknowledged messages per channel.
Queues can be durable or transient, exclusive or auto-deleted. Message persistence depends on the message's own delivery mode, not only on the queue or exchange being durable.

entries.name: NATS
entries.summary: An open source messaging system: subject based publish/subscribe and request/reply, persistence through JetStream, and leaf nodes and superclusters to extend across clouds. CNCF incubating.

cncf.text: NATS was accepted to CNCF on March 15, 2018 at the Incubating maturity level.

version.name: nats-server
version.docs: nats.io about page and GitHub releases

notes: The about page does not describe clustering, subjects or JetStream in detail (unconfirmed beyond the one-line descriptions).

sections.title: What it is
items: Ships as a single lightweight binary with official clients in many languages. Supports publish/subscribe and request/reply, routes messages by subject, and offers persistent streaming through JetStream.
Leaf nodes and superclusters let teams add new clouds, regions or edge sites over time. The page does not describe clustering in detail. The server and clients are Apache 2.0.

entries.name: Apache Cassandra
entries.summary: A distributed database with no single master: data placed on a token ring by consistent hashing, replicated to several nodes, with gossip for membership.

started.basis: GitHub repository created (the project is older: unconfirmed)

cncf.text: An Apache Software Foundation project, not a CNCF project.

version.name: Apache Cassandra
version.docs: cassandra.apache.org download page (latest GA 5.0, release 5.0.9 on 2026-08-07) and the 5.0 architecture docs

notes: GitHub has tags (cassandra-5.0.9) but no GitHub releases, so no automatic release check runs. The docs page read is labelled prerelease on the page itself.
The page does not use the words peer-to-peer or no master.

sections.title: Architecture
items: Partitioning by consistent hashing on a token ring, replication by strategy and factor, multi-master writes with versioned data and tunable consistency, last-write-wins by per-column timestamp.
Gossip shares node state. Each node's phi accrual failure detector marks peers up or down. Repair: read repair, hinted handoff, anti-entropy repair with Merkle trees.
See the Ring tab for the details.

entries.name: Prometheus
entries.summary: A monitoring system. Federation lets one Prometheus scrape selected series from others, which gives a hierarchy. CNCF graduated.

cncf.text: Prometheus was accepted to CNCF on May 9, 2016 at the Incubating maturity level and moved to the Graduated maturity level on August 9, 2018.

notes: The federation page shows no Prometheus version. The version is the latest GitHub release. Start date is the oldest GitHub release. Which setups still need federation versus remote write was not read (unconfirmed).

sections.title: Federation
items: Hierarchical federation: higher-level servers collect aggregated data from many subordinate servers, to scale across many data centers. Cross-service federation: one service's Prometheus pulls selected metrics from another's so both datasets can be queried and alerted on together.

Every Prometheus has a /federate endpoint. A request needs at least one match[] parameter holding an instant vector selector such as up or {job="api-server"}. Several matchers are combined. Set honor_labels on the scraping server to keep the source labels.
